solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Case of equerry covering up certain bet on horse — fraudulent practice

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece sitting on another follows it, so the pieces join end to end

parts.note: a mount is a horse for riding

indicators.note: to cover something up is to wrap around it, so one piece encloses another
a case is the outside of something, so only the outermost letters of the word are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of the word
in betting a banker is a selection considered certain to win

explanation.surface: A royal attendant is caught hiding a sure-thing wager on a racehorse, which smells of fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covering up' sounds like concealment in a scandal, but it is the container signal. A banker is British betting slang for a near-certain winner.
explanation.definitionFit: A mountebank is a travelling quack or charlatan, so his trickery or swindling is the fraudulent practice named here.

clue.text: A simple logo designed for urban complex

indicators.note: something designed has been planned and laid out afresh, so the letters are put into a new arrangement

parts.note: all eleven letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A graphic designer produces a plain logo for a large city development.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Designed' reads naturally as the logo being drawn up, but it tells you to rearrange the letters of the first three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A megalopolis is a vast sprawling city or chain of merged cities, a very large conurbation.

clue.text: Reporting to Cardinal Newman, umpteen leaders upset

indicators.note: in a down clue, to upset something is to tip it over so it reads from the bottom upwards

parts.note: cardinal is a deep red colour, after the robes cardinals wear

indicators.note: leaders are those at the front, so only the first letter of each word is taken

parts.note: the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Cardinal Newman's many subordinates are said to be upset about who they answer to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal Newman' looks like one person but splits: Cardinal is the colour RED and Newman supplies only its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone working under a manager reports to that person; the preposition expresses the same subordinate position in a hierarchy.

clue.text: Doodah, fine and tacky

parts.note: fine as in a fine thread, slender
tacky as in sticky

explanation.surface: A throwaway remark calling some gadget fine but cheap and tasteless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' and 'tacky' both suggest judgements of quality, but here they mean slender and sticky.
explanation.definitionFit: Doodah and thingummy are both colloquial placeholder words for an object whose name escapes the speaker.

clue.text: Guzzler eating seconds gets support

indicators.note: whatever is eaten ends up inside the eater, so one piece is taken inside another

parts.note: one who bolts food, wolfing it down
s is the abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: A glutton going back for second helpings is somehow backed up for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seconds' suggests extra helpings, fitting the guzzler, but it is just the unit abbreviation S.
explanation.definitionFit: To bolster is to prop up or reinforce, and as a noun it is a long pillow giving physical support.

clue.text: Permission to house parent, one of no fixed abode?

indicators.note: to house something is to give it a home inside, so one piece shelters another

parts.note: a nod is a sign of approval, the go-ahead
ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: Asking leave to put up a parent who is otherwise homeless.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the homeless one is housed inside the answer; the question mark flags the definition as playful.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomad wanders from place to place with no permanent residence, which is exactly having no settled home.

clue.text: Bound to tour Italian capital, English seaside town and northern European city

indicators.note: a tour goes all the way around, so one piece circles another

parts.note: a bound is a limit or boundary, an end

indicators.note: a capital letter stands at the head of a word, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the word's first letter
Hove is a resort on the Sussex coast, next to Brighton
N is the standard abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: A travel itinerary: obliged to take in Rome, an English resort and a city in northern Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italian capital' begs to be Rome, but it is only the capital letter of Italian. Hove is a seaside town in East Sussex, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Eindhoven is a major city in the southern Netherlands, known for Philips and its technology industry.

clue.text: Still against the policy, all ends up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom to the top
the end of each word is its final letter, so the last letter of every word is kept

parts.note: the last letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: Someone still opposes the policy, and everything ends in an uproar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All ends' covers every word in 'against the policy', not just the last one.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adverbs mean even now or up to this time, as in 'not finished still' and 'not finished yet'.

clue.text: Old oath, say: a "damn" originally?

parts.note: e.g. means for example, which is what 'say' means here
taken as written

indicators.note: originally means at the origin or start, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Wondering whether some archaic curse was once simply a swear word like damn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like it introduces an example of an oath; it is the abbreviation EG.
explanation.definitionFit: Egad is an archaic mild exclamation, probably a softened form of 'ah God', used as a minced swear.

clue.text: Light visibly green? Ponder heading off

indicators.note: with its head taken off, a word loses its first letter

parts.note: looking green about the gills means looking sick
ruminate means ponder; its first letter goes

explanation.surface: A question about whether a light shows green, then an instruction to think while setting off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' seems to go with 'green' as a traffic light, but it is a verb, the definition. RUMINATE loses its R.
explanation.definitionFit: To illuminate something is to shine light on it, so the verb is a direct synonym for lighting it.

clue.text: Fair — though one-sided?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, whimsical: entirely on the right-hand side

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is a pun: something wholly on the right has only one side; the question mark flags the play.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair in the sense of middling or acceptable matches the everyday meaning of satisfactory, good enough.

clue.text: Hearts captured by artist with a flower

indicators.note: a captive is held inside by its captor, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: Salvador Dali, the surrealist painter
H is the card-suit abbreviation for hearts
taken as written

explanation.surface: A painter wins people over by bringing along a bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: The artist could be RA, the usual crossword artist, but a painter's name is needed here to hold the H.
explanation.definitionFit: The dahlia is a showy garden plant of the daisy family, grown for its large bright blooms.

clue.text: Wearing underwear, one means to access study

parts.note: wearing a vest is being in a vest
the Roman numeral for one
a gate is a way in

explanation.surface: Someone in their undies finds a way into a private room.
explanation.walkthrough: A vest is British for an undershirt, so 'wearing underwear' is IN VEST. 'Study' looks like the room being entered, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To study a matter is to examine it carefully, and investigating is looking into it systematically.

clue.text: Stuffed — like a koala perhaps?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in serious trouble, done for
second meaning, literal: sitting high in a eucalyptus

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuffed' suggests a full belly or a stuffed toy koala; it means in a fix. Koalas live and feed in eucalyptus, also called gum trees.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means stuck in a difficult position with no escape, which is British slang for being stuffed.

clue.text: Country — almost entire nation tucking into fancy gateau

indicators.note: almost all of something is one short of the whole, so the final letter is dropped
food being tucked into goes inside the eater, so one piece goes within another
fancy means elaborate or fanciful, so the letters are dressed up in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
Mali, a whole country named in one word, without its final letter

explanation.surface: Nearly a whole country tucking into an elaborate cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entire nation' is simply a nation, MALI, clipped by 'almost'; the rearranged cake letters wrap round the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Guatemala is a republic in Central America, bordering Mexico, Belize, Honduras and El Salvador.

clue.text: Spinner a long way off, old, old, flat surface beginning to turn

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
O is the abbreviation for old
a plane is a flat surface in geometry

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the word's first letter

explanation.surface: A spinning top far away on some old flat table, just starting to rotate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spinner' suggests a cricket bowler or a top; it is a planet spinning on its axis. The two 'old's give different abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: An exoplanet orbits a star other than our sun, so it is a rotating world at an immense distance.

clue.text: Boy or girl with a word of support

parts.note: Viv is short for Vivian or Vivien, used for either sex
taken as written

explanation.surface: A child offering encouragement.
explanation.walkthrough: The name has to suit either sex, which is why the clue says 'boy or girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: Viva is an Italian and Spanish cheer meaning 'long live', shouted in acclaim of a person or cause.

clue.text: Fold in garment cut for suit

indicators.note: cutting something short trims its end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: a pleat is a fold sewn into cloth, here without its last letter

explanation.surface: A dressmaker's note: a tuck made in clothing trimmed to make a jacket and trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' looks like tailoring, fitting the garment, but it means a petition.
explanation.definitionFit: A suit in the old sense is an appeal or petition, as in pressing one's suit, which is an earnest request.

clue.text: Awfully swollen cuts certainly a symptom of jaundice

indicators.note: a cut goes into something, so one piece is slotted inside another

parts.note: yes, certainly: an emphatic agreement

indicators.note: awfully means badly done, so the letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A medical note: badly swollen wounds are certainly a sign of liver trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuts' reads as wounds, but it is a verb telling the rearranged letters to cut into YES.
explanation.definitionFit: Jaundice turns the skin and eyes a yellowish colour, so that tint is its best-known visible sign.

clue.text: Nation lush and hot, one in twelve assumes

indicators.note: to assume is to take on, so one piece takes others inside it

parts.note: Leo is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac
a lush is a drunkard, as is a sot
H is the tap abbreviation for hot

explanation.surface: Describing a country as verdant and warm, with one in twelve of the populace making assumptions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lush and hot' read like a description of the nation's climate; lush is a noun here, a drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Lesotho is a small mountainous kingdom in southern Africa, entirely surrounded by South Africa.

clue.text: Ultimately, mourners aren't travelling to the wake?

indicators.note: things that travel move about, so the letters change places
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the word's last letter
taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: In the end, the grieving family won't be going to the gathering after the funeral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wake' seems to be the vigil after a death, fitting mourners, but it is the track left behind a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Astern is nautical for towards the back of a vessel, which is where its wake trails behind it.

clue.text: Creatures with one foot but no head, tough things

indicators.note: with no head, a word has lost its first letter

parts.note: snails move on a single muscular foot; the first letter is dropped

explanation.surface: Describing hardy one-footed, headless creatures.
explanation.walkthrough: Gastropods such as snails glide on one muscular underside called a foot.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'hard as nails' makes these metal fasteners the byword for toughness, and a tough person is said to be nails.

clue.text: Learner in pass, papers outstanding

indicators.note: a piece that is in another sits within it

parts.note: to pass time is to spend it
L is the learner-driver plate
ID means identity papers

explanation.surface: A learner driver passes the test, but the paperwork is still pending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass' and 'outstanding' suggest a driving test and unfinished paperwork, but pass is a verb and outstanding is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Outstanding means excellent or remarkable, and splendid is praise for something magnificent or very fine.

clue.text: Opera in Carmen or Manon

indicators.note: the answer is contained within the run of words that follows

parts.note: spans the end of the first word, the whole second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Pondering which opera a character appears in, Bizet's or Massenet's.
explanation.walkthrough: Carmen and Manon are both operas, tempting a choice between them; the answer is a third one sitting across their letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Norma is Bellini's tragic opera of 1831 about a Druid priestess, one of the great bel canto works.

clue.text: Spirit knocked back slightly, figure appearing wretched

indicators.note: knocked back means sent backwards, so the letters run in reverse

parts.note: an elf is a sprite, a spirit of folklore
slightly means a bit
ten is a number, a figure

explanation.surface: After drinking a little too much, someone looks miserable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit knocked back' suggests downing a drink, but the spirit is a sprite, reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Flea-bitten literally means infested with fleas, and by extension shabby, squalid and miserable-looking.

clue.text: European army officer holds permit

indicators.note: whatever is held is gripped within, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: Lt is the abbreviation for lieutenant
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A continental army officer has a pass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Permit' looks like a noun the officer holds, but it is the verb and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To let someone do something is to allow it, so the two verbs are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Sounding natural, laugh heartily

indicators.note: sounding means as heard, so the word is judged by its pronunciation

parts.note: raw means unrefined, in a natural state; in British speech the two words are pronounced the same

explanation.surface: Laughing unaffectedly and loudly.
explanation.walkthrough: The homophone relies on a non-rhotic accent, where the final R is not pronounced.
explanation.definitionFit: To roar with laughter is to laugh loudly and without restraint, so the verb alone carries that sense.

clue.text: Establishment by the way can't fear moves to host game

indicators.note: a host takes guests in, so one piece holds another inside
things that move shift position, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe ignored
a sport is a game

explanation.surface: A business nearby whose fearless owner decides to stage a match.
explanation.walkthrough: A transport cafe is British for a roadside diner used by lorry drivers. 'By the way' reads as an aside but means beside the road.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a cheap eatery on a main road catering to truckers, literally a business beside the highway.
